items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: Well my two main teachers were Big Sid Catlett and Jo Jones.

ctx.x: It was something I read in one of these jazz books and I just felt I had to ask you about that.

Yeah. Well my two main teachers were Big Sid Catlett and Jo Jones. I had a chance to see Chick [Webb] once but Big Sid and Jo really called me aside and said “look, here’s how you play the brushes, here’s how you do this, here’s how you do this, and always remember, don’t ever lose one.” You know I learned that from Dizzy too. What they meant was when you play a four bar break, make sure everybody knows where one is. Because once you lose one, two three and four is gone and it never comes back.

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: During one of the intermissions, Big Sid said, “Come here, kid.” He said, “Here’s how you play the hi-hat.

ctx.x: Oh, Big Sid Catlett. He would take me – I remember going to Atlantic City to hear Benny Goodman’s band. Big Sid was playing with Benny. During one of the intermissions, Big Sid said, “Come here, kid.” He said, “Here’s how you play the hi-hat.” You’ve got to have a special touch for the hi-hat. “Here’s how you play the brushes.” That guy was a champ with the brushes, Jo Jones. He came into the nightclub with Bobby Cranshaw. Quartet. John Bunch on piano and Ted Nash on saxophone. Let me tell you. He came in with a…
It sounds like the drummers was a fraternity of sorts. It sounds like you guys had a real rapport and looked out for one another? Is that really the case?
